title: Hanging and Weighing
theme: The root pend/pens: hanging, weighing and paying out
objectives: I can explain how the root pend/pens (hang, weigh) connects ten words that seem unrelated.
I can use the prefix and the root to work out the meaning of an unfamiliar word.
I can choose the right word for hanging, relying, paying out, giving out, and thinking.
I can use words from the unit to write about a scene in a workshop.
rationale: Pend/pens joins ideas that seem unrelated (a clock's pendulum, depending on a friend, compensating for a loss) through one image of hanging and weighing, which makes it a strong test of root reasoning. The ten words are grouped by the meaning that grew from the root: hanging and swinging, weighing out and paying, hanging on or leaning on, and weighing thoughts. Each word also has a prefix or suffix, so students practice breaking a word into parts and checking the meaning against context. The same habit works for the next two root units (mit/miss and struct).

words.def: A weight hanging from a fixed point that swings back and forth.
words.ex: The heavy pendulum in the grandfather clock swung back and forth all day.
words.ex2: In science class, we timed how long a pendulum took to swing back and forth ten times.
words.nonExample: A ball lying on the floor is not a pendulum.

apps.academic: Scientists use a pendulum to study how motion repeats.
apps.writing: Use pendulum for a hanging weight; public opinion is sometimes said to swing like a pendulum.

words.def: To need or rely on someone or something.

passage.title: The Clock Shop
paras: On Saturday, Noor visited her great-uncle Tariq's clock shop, where dozens of clocks ticked at once. Above the workbench hung an old wall clock with a long brass pendulum that swung from side to side. "Every clock in here depends on that swing," Tariq said. "Without it, this one cannot keep time."

Tariq had suspended a small silver pendant from the hook above his bench, and it turned slowly in the draft. Noor was still watching it when thunder rumbled outside. The radio had warned of an impending storm, and her great-uncle's face grew pensive.

"Storms mean power cuts," he said, "and my customers need their clocks working by Monday. Fixing six of them will expend all my energy this weekend." Noor offered to help. She opened the repair manual and turned to the appendix, where a chart listed the right pendulum length for each clock. "This one needs a shorter pendulum," she read aloud.

Tariq nodded and dispensed a single drop of oil onto each gear while Noor checked the numbers. Rain tapped on the windows, and one by one the clocks fell quiet and then started ticking again in the right rhythm. By evening, all six were finished.

"Let me compensate you for your hard work," Tariq said, reaching for his wallet. Noor shook her head. "You don't need to. I learned how time is kept." Tariq laughed, and above them the pendant swung again as the storm broke.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "impending" most nearly means
choices: unexpected and silly
far away in the future
about to happen soon
easy to repair
qs.why: The radio warned of a storm and thunder had already begun, so the storm was about to arrive.

qs.q: Why does Tariq's face become pensive?
choices: He is angry at Noor for visiting.
He is thinking about how much work the storm will cause.
He has lost his silver pendant.
He is trying to remember a song.
qs.why: He says storms mean power cuts and that the clocks must be ready by Monday, so he is thinking about the work ahead.

qs.q: Which detail best shows how important the pendulum is to the clock?
choices: A silver pendant hangs from the hook.
Noor reads from the repair manual.
Tariq says the clock depends on its swing and cannot keep time without it.
Rain taps on the windows.
qs.why: Tariq states directly that the clock cannot keep time without the swinging pendulum.

qs.q: Why does Noor tell her great-uncle he does not need to compensate her?
choices: She feels that learning how time is kept was reward enough.
She was paid earlier in the day.
She thinks the work was easy.
She wants to take the clocks home.
qs.why: Noor says she learned how time is kept, which shows she values the experience more than payment.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Clocks cannot be repaired during storms.
Pendants are more valuable than clocks.
Working together can solve a problem and teach something worth more than money.
Repair manuals are always out of date.
qs.why: Noor and Tariq finish the work together, and Noor says what she gained was learning.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words built on the root pend/pens, use the picture of hanging and weighing to connect them, read a scene in a clock shop, and practice breaking words into prefix, root, and ending.

notes.va.pendulum.n: Anchor word for the unit: the weight hangs, so pend = hang. Let students make a pendulum from a string and a washer. The ending -ulum is a noun ending from Latin; do not make students analyze it further.
notes.va.suspend.v: The second sense (stopping for a time) comes from the picture of something left hanging in the air. Connect it to suspense, which is the feeling of waiting. Students may only know the school-discipline sense; widen it.
notes.va.appendix.n: An appendix hangs on the end of a book: ap- (to, onto) plus pend (hang), with a noun ending -ix. The body sense (a small part attached to the intestine) uses the same picture of something that hangs on. The plural is appendices (or appendixes).
notes.va.impending.adj: The picture is something hanging over you that is about to drop. Be sure students separate this im- ('upon') from the im- ('not') in unit 3. Impending usually modifies events such as storms, deadlines, and changes.
notes.va.depend.v: The picture: something hangs from something else, so it relies on it. Use a mobile or a hanging plant. Students rarely connect depend to pendulum until you draw it.
notes.va.compensate.v: The picture is a scale: compensate means to weigh things against each other until they balance. Use two cups and coins to show it. Students may think compensate only means paying money; it also means balancing a problem by effort.
notes.va.dispense.v: Dispense is giving out in portions, as if each portion were weighed. Machines, pharmacists, and volunteers dispense. The phrase dispense with (do without) is a separate idiom; mention it but do not assess it.
notes.va.expend.v: Expend and spend are close in sound and meaning; expend is more formal and works for energy and effort as well as money. Link to expense and expenditure.
notes.va.pensive.adj: A pensive person is weighing thoughts in the mind. Link to pensar in Spanish for students who know it. Pensive is not the same as sad; it is quiet thinking that may or may not be sad.
notes.va.pendant.n: A pendant is a thing that hangs. Compare with pending (waiting to be decided) and pendent; students often mix the endings -ant and -ent. A short spelling routine: pendant, the noun, ends like 'ant'.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Compensate. I see com- meaning together, pens meaning weigh, and -ate that makes a verb. If I weigh two things together, I can make them balance. That fits: to compensate is to make up for a loss so things balance.'

needsReview: Etymology and word-part meanings to verify with a linguistics-informed reviewer: pend as 'hang' and 'weigh' (Latin pendere); pens as the same root; prefix meanings sus- ('up, from below'), ap- ('to, onto'), im- ('upon'), de- ('down, from'), ex- ('out'), com- ('together'), dis- ('apart, out'); the noun endings -ulum and -ix are mentioned only in teacher notes as noun endings (no word-part breakdown is shown for pendulum or appendix); -ant glossed as 'a thing that'. No further etymological claims are made.
Teacher note and morph meaning for expend ('weigh, pay') assume the weighing-to-paying link; confirm the wording.
Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: colgar (suspend), repartir (dispense; 'dispensar' also exists), gastar (expend), inminente, colgante, apéndice, péndulo.

Fact claims in word records: pendulum clocks keep time by a swinging pendulum; a shorter pendulum swings faster; an appendix is a small part attached to the intestines; suspension bridges hang the road from cables; prescription medicine is dispensed to the person it was written for; archaeologists have found pendants of shell, bone, and stone.
Sense boundary: suspend (stop for a time), appendix (body part), depend (be decided by), and dispense (dispense with) are second senses; confirm they help rather than distract.
